EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of power outages and traffic accidents. One traffic accident resulted in the death of a boy in Pittsylvania County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 3.9 inches of snow, up to 2.0 inches of sleet, and up to 0.50 inches of freezing rain. Key Impacts: traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions were introduced across the North Carolina and Virginia Piedmonts in early January after the previous two months of November and December recorded precipitation totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, which ended up being 25 to 50 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November and December, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd to 5th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 6th of January. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moved eastward along the Gulf Coast on January 30 and intensified as it reached the Georgia and South Carolina coastline by January 31. This single low pressure system combined with Arctic air to the north to produce a Miller A winter storm where all precipitation fell as snow due to the absence of any warm nose aloft. Snow totals ranged from about four inches to eight inches south of Route 460, but drier air to the north caused a sharp gradient where totals dropped significantly. Impacts from this storm were mainly transportation delays as power outages were limited due to the snow being dry and fluffy.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow totals reached 5.0 inches. Key Impacts: transportation delays.

Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Dan river, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moved eastward along the Gulf Coast on January 30 and intensified as it reached the Georgia and South Carolina coastline by January 31. This single low pressure system combined with Arctic air to the north to produce a Miller A winter storm where all precipitation fell as snow due to the absence of any warm nose aloft. Snow totals ranged from about four inches to eight inches south of Route 460, but drier air to the north caused a sharp gradient where totals dropped significantly. Impacts from this storm were mainly transportation delays as power outages were limited due to the snow being dry and fluffy.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow totals ranged from 3.0 to 7.0 inches. Key Impacts: transportation delays.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across the eastern Panhandle of West Virginia. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 6 to 12. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a quarter of an inch were observed as well. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state. Sleet avalanches were reported across the mountains which buried roads with upwards of 10 feet of sleet closing them for days.

An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of power outages and traffic accidents. One traffic accident resulted in the death of a boy in Pittsylvania County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 2.0 inches of snow, up to 2.8 inches of sleet, and up to 0.50 inches of freezing rain. Key Impacts: power outages, traffic accidents.

The end of January rounded out with accumulating snow showers across southwestern Virginia in response to a passing low pressure system. The center of this disturbance intensified over the Carolinas on January 30th, pulling an abundance of moisture up from the south. Colder air ushered in from the north set the stage for precipitation to fall as snow as this event got underway on the morning of the 30th. The track of the storm kept the bulk of measurable snow contained within the southern coalfields and eastward into the Mid-Atlantic region before wrapping up by the later half of the day on January 31st. For Buchanan and Dickenson Counties, six to seven inches of snow fell across the highest elevations and between three to five inches for the lower elevations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rather anomalous Arctic Outbreak settled in ahead of the January 25th Winter Storm with reinforcing shots through the last week of January. The remarkable aspect of this outbreak was the duration, especially for the Mid-Atlantic. The coldest nights (January 27th, 30th, and 31st) featured Extreme Cold Warnings. The coldest wind chills were overnight.

Severe Drought conditions were introduced across the North Carolina and Virginia Piedmonts in early January after the previous two months of November and December recorded precipitation totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, which ended up being 25 to 50 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November and December, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd to 5th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 6th of January. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November and December, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 5th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 6th of January. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Roanoke river, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website.

As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down on Saddle Hollow Road near Mint Spring Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front crossed the Mid-Atlantic during the early morning hours. A band of showers and a few thunderstorms developed along it. Although most of the region remained stable near the surface, a small area of the central Shenandoah Valley into the central Virginia piedmont remained just unstable enough to allow for a few severe downbursts, including one significant gust just south of the City of Staunton shortly after 4 AM EDT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A significant localized wind gust affected the Jolivue area just south of the City of Staunton. Shingles were peeled off the roof of a home in the unit block of Chesnut Road. Surrounding properties in the neighborhood had dozens of trees (mostly pine trees) uprooted and snapped, all laying in a general southeastward direction in line with the parent storm motion.

A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous large trees fell down and snapped in the Salisbury neighborhood in Midlothian.

A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind gust of 54 knots (62 MPH) was measured by the AWOS at Quantico Marine Base (KNYG).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Just before dawn on March 16th, strong thunderstorms passed through southwest Virginia along a cold front. A period of damaging wind gusts took place across Buchanan County as the storms swept through, causing tree and power line damage in the communities of Rowe and Thomas. In the wake of the cold front, freezing temperatures festered over the area and set forth a period of winter weather across southwest Virginia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees were knocked down along Thomas Mountain Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: One last burst of winter weather for the season took place across southwest Virginia beginning on the afternoon of March 16th in the wake of a cold front. A surge of sub-freezing temperatures sweeping into the area on the backside of the front resulted in a transition from rain to snow. Snow showers progressed into the afternoon of March 17th before building high pressure promoted the return of quiet weather. In the midst of the snow, an average of one to three inches of snow fell across Buchanan and Dickenson Counties, with locally higher amounts taking place along the higher elevations.

A quasi-stationary front drifted into northern Virginia, supported aloft by a weak upper level trough, provided instability for a few severe thunderstorms to develop. Lapse rates of around 6-7 degrees C/km and CAPE values between 1000-2000 J/kg were observed, in addition to afternoon surface temperatures in the 80s, triggered thunderstorms that produced large hail along the Blue Ridge into the Piedmont.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail of around 1 inch in diameter was observed along Wheats Valley Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching cold front, supported by an upper-level shortwave trough, triggered widely scattered thunderstorms. Decreasing cloud cover during late afternoon allowed instability to increase, with CAPE values in Blacksburg, VA reaching as high as 3,000 J/Kg per the 30/00z upper air sounding. Lapse rates were observed near 7 C/km, while 0-1km shear was observed at around 40 knots. Storms developed along the Blue Ridge and pushed east into the Piedmont, increasing in intensity across the southern Piedmont. Storms then congealed into a broken line that tracked southeast. Although no hail was reported, there were several reports of trees blown down by thunderstorm winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds blew down about 8 trees near intersection of Alton Post Office Road and Dawson Trail.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light snow fell in Lee County, with 3.7 inches measured in Jonesville and 2 inches measured in Ewing.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A combination of a period of warm weather in March allowing for crops to bud earlier than normal and a late April hard freeze resulted in widespread crop damage and loss across portions of the Piedmont on April 21.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A late season freeze occurred during the morning hours of April 21 in New Kent County. Temperatures dropped as low as 29 degrees Fahrenheit at the New Kent County ASOS. This led to significant crop loss across the county. One winery lost 90 percent of their grapes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A combination of a period of warm weather in March allowing for crops to bud earlier than normal and a late April hard freeze resulted in widespread crop damage and loss across portions of the Piedmont on April 21.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A late season freeze occurred during the morning hours of April 21 in Louisa County. Temperatures dropped as low as 25 degrees Fahrenheit at the Louisa County ASOS. This led to significant crop loss of grapes across the county. According to the Virginia Wineries Association, wineries statewide reported crop losses as high as 80-90 percent. One winery in Louisa County reported at least 50 percent crop loss of grapes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April began with widespread moderate drought (D1) conditions already present across Buchanan and Dickenson Counties. Although around an inch of rain fell during the first week of the month, it was not enough to improve conditions. This was followed by relatively dry weather, which allowed for a further degradation to a severe drought (D2) by the third week of the month. Showers and storms brought some additional precipitation during the third and fourth weeks of the month, but once again did nothing to improve or resolve the D2 state in Buchanan and Dickenson.||Impacts included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions expanded into Carroll county in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the New River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening of the May 27th across central and southwest Virginia as a strong upper level disturbance passed across the lower Mid-Atlantic along a stationary front draped across the region. The storms developed in a moderately unstable environment, with surface temperatures observed in the low to mid 80s during the afternoon, while dewpoints were observed in the upper 60s to low 70s. This helped to drive MLCAPE values into the 1,500 to 2,000 J/kg range, with relatively steep low-level lapse rates. Area wind profilers also indicated westerly winds within the low levels of the atmosphere, with 30-35 kt of deep-layer shear supporting damaging wind gusts in the stronger thunderstorm activity.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds along South Constitution Highway.

These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions continued in Bland county in May after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Deep moisture pooled across the lower Mid-Atlantic during the afternoon and evening of the 25th ahead of a slow-moving cold front situated near the Ohio River, with precipitable water values reaching into the 1.8 to 1.9 inch range across the Southside area of Virginia per Storm Prediction Center Meso-analysis. Abundant daytime heating allowed CAPE values to reach in excess of 1,500 J/kg during the evening. A line of slow-moving thunderstorms developed along a nearly-stationary surface trough that extended from Carroll County through central Halifax and Charlotte Counties, with multiple cells observed training along this boundary. The heaviest rain was observed within the Polecat Creek and Miry Creek basins, where nearly 5.5 inches fell within a 3-hour period. Multiple cells were estimated by radar to be producing rainfall rates of 3 to 5 inches per hour. Cells began to develop over the basins at around 6:00 pm EDT, with training reaching a maximum at around 8:00 pm EDT. Despite dry antecedent conditions with D3: Extreme Drought highlighted for all of Halifax County by the U.S. Drought Monitor, MRMS FLASH data estimated the rainfall reached the 200-year Average Recurrence Interval ceiling for a 3-hour duration along a east-west strip within the west-central portion of the county, with rainfall totals reaching 150 percent of the 3-hour Flash Flood Guidance. CREST Unit Streamflow ranged from 350 to 650 cfs per mi^2 during the storm.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Chatham Road was observed flooded and impassible as heavy rain caused Polecat Creek to rise out of its banks several inches deep across the roadway surface.  No damage was observed to the road, which was reopened to traffic after the flooding receded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Deep moisture pooled across the lower Mid-Atlantic during the afternoon and evening of the 26th to the south of a stationary front draped across northern Virginia. Precipitable water values were estimated in the 1.8 to 1.9 inch range across the New River Valley area of Virginia per Storm Prediction Center Meso-analysis, while CAPE values were estimated to range from 1,500 to 2,000 J/kg during the evening. A series of thunderstorms were observed training across the southern half of Pulaski County, VA beginning around 6 PM EDT, with cells passing from west to east across the area through 9 PM EDT. Multiple cells were estimated by radar to have produced rainfall rates of 3 to 4 inches per hour. Dry antecedent conditions were noted for all of Pulaski County, with D2: Severe Drought highlighted by the U.S. Drought Monitor.  It was estimated that between 4 and 6 inches or rain fell within the headwaters of Big Macks Creek.  MRMS FLASH did not present impressive returns, and was offset from the Big Macks Creek basin by 3-5 miles to the west. FLASH estimated the rainfall reached into the 50 to 70-year Average Recurrence Interval range for a 6-hour duration along a narrow north to south strip west of the basin, with rainfall totals reaching 180 percent of the 6-hour Flash Flood Guidance. CREST Unit Streamflow ranged from 125 to 250 cfs per mi^2 during the event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A total of 4 to 6 inches of rain fell within the headwaters of Big Macks Creek.  Of this total,  3 to 5 inches of rain fell in 1.5 hours.  Max Creek Road was impassible, with 2 of the 7 bridges leading into Camp Powhatan sustaining damage. The estimated water depth in Big Macks Creek was 9 feet higher than base flow.  Debris was observed having been washed onto some of the bridges.  Runoff caused Lake Powhatan to rise 3 to 4 feet.

These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions expanded into Grayson county in early May after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the New River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A significant and highly damaging ice storm unfolded in Washington County VA as temperatures struggled to get to 32F or above, especially in the northeastern portion of the county. Ice accretion ranged from 0.25 to 0.50 inches across the county, resulting in significant damage. A trained spotter reported a maximum of 0.75 inch in the Emory and Meadowview areas, these locations stayed below freezing for a significant period of time. Extensive utility damage occurred, with power poles, powerlines, and transformers breaking from either ice weight outright or collapse of trees. At least 45% of the county was without power by the evening on the 25th. Snow and sleet accumulations of 0.8 inches near Bristol and 2.0 inches at the coop in Abingdon were also recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Alberta Clipper brought a period of moderate snow during the afternoon and early evening hours of February 6th. This tapered to light snow through the evening. Between 11 PM February 6th and 2 AM February 7th, a potent snow squall moved through along an Arctic Front. This reduced visibilities below one quarter of a mile, wind gusts to 50 mph, and quick accumulations near 1-2 in about 30 minutes. By the time the snow ended, total accumulations of 2 to 5 were observed. Winds gusted to 50 mph through the day of February 7th resulting in significant blowing and drifting of snow. Several roads were reported drifted shut.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Nor'Easter moved northward along the Eastern Seaboard February 22nd into the 23rd. Temperatures were marginal to start outside of elevation, making the snowfall totals elevation dependent. This storm was unique as it had several local maxima across the state. The greatest amounts were in along the Blue Ridge where 4 to locally 12 inches were observed. Higher terrain in the Shenandoah Valley also received localized totals of 2 to 6 inches. In western Highland County, the upslope snow continued longer resulting in 4 to 10 inches. Across northern Virginia, a general 2 to 5 inches were observed.
